lesson.title: Same Sign, Bigger Signal: The Non-Inverting Amplifier
lesson.summary: The non-inverting amplifier applies the input directly to the op-amp's high-impedance non-inverting input and uses a resistor divider in the feedback path to set a gain of 1 + R2/R1, producing an output that is in phase with the input.
lesson.body:
The non-inverting amplifier solves the input impedance limitation left at the end of the inverting amplifier chapter. Instead of routing the input signal through a resistor into the inverting input, the input voltage Vin is applied directly to the non-inverting input, V+, which under the ideal op-amp assumptions draws essentially zero current. A feedback resistor R2 connects the output to the inverting input, V-, and a second resistor R1 connects that same V- node down to ground, forming a voltage divider that samples a fraction of the output back to V-.

The virtual short from earlier in this unit gives V- = V+ = Vin directly; there is no virtual ground here, since V+ is not tied to ground, it is driven by the actual signal. The current flowing from the V- node down through R1 to ground is, by Ohm's law, I1 = V- / R1 = Vin / R1. As in the inverting case, none of this current can be supplied by the op-amp's input terminal (infinite input impedance), so it must instead be supplied entirely through R2 from the output. Writing that same current through R2, from Vout down to V-: I2 = (Vout minus V-) / R2. Setting I1 = I2: Vin / R1 = (Vout minus Vin) / R2, which rearranges to Vout minus Vin = Vin times R2 / R1, and finally Vout = Vin times (1 + R2 / R1). The closed-loop voltage gain is Av = 1 + R2 / R1.

Two features distinguish this result from the inverting amplifier's gain of negative R2 / R1. First, there is no minus sign: the output is in phase with the input, not inverted. Second, the gain is always at least 1, since R2 / R1 cannot be negative for positive resistor values, so this topology can never attenuate a signal, only leave it unchanged or amplify it.

As a worked example, let R1 = 2 kilohms and R2 = 8 kilohms, with Vin = 1 V. The gain is Av = 1 + 8 kilohms / 2 kilohms = 1 + 4 = 5, so Vout = 5 times 1 V = 5 V. Checking with the current method: V- = Vin = 1 V by the virtual short. The current through R1 is I1 = 1 V / 2000 ohms = 0.0005 A, or 0.5 mA, flowing down to ground. The same 0.5 mA must flow through R2, from Vout down to V-, producing a voltage drop of 0.0005 A times 8000 ohms = 4 V across R2. Since Vout is 4 V higher than V- (current flows from the higher potential Vout down through R2 to V-), Vout = V- + 4 V = 1 V + 4 V = 5 V, matching the formula.

Because the source now drives V+ directly rather than driving current through an input resistor, the input impedance seen by the source is the op-amp's own extremely high input impedance, not a designer-chosen resistor value, which is exactly the advantage this topology offers over the inverting amplifier. Pushing this idea to its logical extreme, what happens if R2 is reduced to zero and R1 is removed entirely, leads directly to the voltage follower, the subject of the next chapter.
